To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) we have shown that it is possible to build a competitive fantasy football manager, 2) the performance of our manager is comparable to that of human managers and 3) our manager can be used to benchmark future research in the area of sequential decision making.

(a) the problem of sequentially optimal team formation in Fantasy Football is a challenging one, (b) it is tractable to build an agent that is competitive in this domain, and (c) the agent can perform well without access to complete information on footballer performances.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a Bayesian reinforcement learning framework for team formation in large partially-observable domains.
how to build a competitive Fantasy Football manager.
the design of algorithms for sequential decision making in domains where the action space grows exponentially with the number of objects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our agent, despite being completely uninformed about the players’ performances, was able to rank at the top of the 2.5 million participants in the competition.
our agent is a competitive Fantasy Football manager, even when competing against human experts, and that the performance of our agent is a strong baseline for future research on this domain.
we present the first realworld benchmark for sequentially optimal team formation, working in the framework of a large, partially-observable domain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it presents the first benchmark for team formation in partially-observable domains and shows that it is possible to achieve state-of-the-art performance in a real-world setting.
we are the first to show how to build an agent which can compete with human experts at Fantasy Football.
we are the first to provide a real-world benchmark in a partially-observable setting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, even without complete access to information, it is possible for a computer agent to compete with humans at a real-world sequential decision making problem.
, even in the absence of complete information on the state of the world, it is possible to build agents that can compete with the best human managers.
, even when faced with a large partially observable domain, sequential decision-making techniques can be used to construct agents that are competitive against human experts.
